{{Short description|Philosophical concept}}
In [[philosophy]], a '''state of affairs''' ({{langx|de|Sachverhalt}}),<ref name="Jesús Padilla Gálvez">{{cite book |last1=Padilla Gálvez |first1=Jesús |title=State of Affairs. Reconstructing the Controversy over Sachverhalt |date=2021 |publisher=Philosophia Verlag |url=https://www.philosophiaverlag.com/shop?store-page=State-of-Affairs-Hardcover-p446462221 |access-date=2023-06-26 |archive-date=2023-01-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230106030031/https://www.philosophiaverlag.com/shop?store-page=State-of-Affairs-Hardcover-p446462221 |url-status=live }}</ref> also known as a '''situation''', is a way the [[actual world]] must be in order to make some given ''[[proposition]]'' about the actual world true; in other words, a state of affairs is a ''truth-maker'', whereas a proposition is a ''truth-bearer''. Whereas states of affairs either ''obtain'' or ''fail-to-obtain'', propositions are either ''true'' or ''false''.<ref name="Textor"/> Some philosophers understand the term "states of affairs" in a more restricted sense as a synonym for "fact". In this sense, there are no states of affairs that do not obtain.<ref name="Textor"/>

The early [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] and [[David Malet Armstrong]] are well known for their defence of a '''factualism'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->, a position according to which the world is a world of facts and not a world of things.<ref>David Armstrong, ''A World of States of Affairs'', Cambridge University Press, 1997, p. 1.</ref>

==Overview==
States of affairs are complex entities: they are built up from or constituted by other entities.<ref name="Borchert2">{{cite book |last1=Borchert |first1=Donald |title=Macmillan Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2nd Edition |date=2006 |publisher=Macmillan |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/MONMEO-3 |chapter=Ontology |access-date=2021-01-14 |archive-date=2021-01-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115121017/https://philpapers.org/rec/MONMEO-3 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Meinertsen |first1=Bo R. |title=Metaphysics of States of Affairs: Truthmaking, Universals, and a Farewell to Bradley's Regress |publisher=Springer Singapore |page=1 |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/MEIMOS-2 |access-date=2021-01-14 |archive-date=2021-01-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111130947/https://philpapers.org/rec/MEIMOS-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> Atomic states of affairs are constituted by one [[particular]] and one [[Properties (philosophy)|property]] exemplified by this particular.<ref name="Sandkühler2">{{cite encyclopedia |language=de|first1=Meinard|last1=Kuhlmann|title=Ontologie (Sec.4:Aktuelle Debatten und Gesamtentwürfe)|editor-last1=Sandkühler |editor-first1=Hans Jörg |encyclopedia=Enzyklopädie Philosophie |date=2010 |publisher=Meiner|doi=10.28937/978-3-7873-3545-9|isbn=978-3-7873-3545-9 }}</ref><ref name="Textor">{{cite web |last1=Textor |first1=Mark |title=States of Affairs |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/states-of-affairs/ |website=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |access-date=9 January 2021 |date=2020 |archive-date=11 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180611161235/https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/states-of-affairs/ |url-status=live }}</ref> For example, the state of affairs that Socrates is wise is constituted by the particular "Socrates" and the property "wise". Relational states of affairs involve several particulars and a relation connecting them. States of affairs that ''obtain'' are also referred to as [[Fact#In philosophy|facts]].<ref name="Textor"/> It is controversial which ontological status should be ascribed to states of affairs that do not obtain.<ref name="Sandkühler2"/> States of affairs have been prominent in 20th-century ontology as various theories were proposed to describe the world as composed of states of affairs.<ref name="Borchert2"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wittgenstein |first1=Ludwig |last2=Colombo |first2=G. C. M. |last3=Russell |first3=Bertrand |title=Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus |date=1922 |publisher=[[Fratelli Bocca]] |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/WITTL-14 |access-date=2021-01-14 |archive-date=2021-01-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111072829/https://philpapers.org/rec/WITTL-14 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Armstrong |first1=D. M. |title=A World of States of Affairs |date=1996 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/ARMAWO-3 |access-date=2021-01-14 |archive-date=2020-11-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201113214856/https://philpapers.org/rec/ARMAWO-3 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In a sense of "state of affairs" favored by [[Ernest Sosa]], states of affairs are situational [[Condition (philosophy)|conditions]]. In fact, in the ''[[Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy]]'',<ref name=Sosa>[[Ernest Sosa]], 1999. "Condition".  ''Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy''.  R.Audi, Ed.  Cambridge: Cambridge UP. p. 171.</ref> Sosa defines a condition to be a state of affairs, "way things are" or situation—most commonly referred to by a [[nominalization]] of a [[sentence (linguistics)|sentence]]. The expression "Snow's being white", which refers to the condition snow's being white, is a nominalization of the sentence "Snow is white".<ref name=Sosa/> The [[truth]] of the proposition that "snow is white" is a nominalization of the sentence "the proposition that snow is white is true". Snow's being white is a necessary and sufficient condition for the truth of the proposition that snow is white. Conditions in this sense may be called situational.

Usually, [[necessity and sufficiency]] relate conditions of the same kind. Being an animal is a necessary attributive condition for being a dog.  Fido's being an animal is a necessary situational condition for Fido's being a dog.
